prize_parts.citation: For the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, enabling atomic clocks with fractional uncertainties near 1e-18

statement.case_for: The optical lattice clock is the clearest case on the shortlist of a new measurement capability that changed what can be measured. Trapping many neutral atoms at the magic wavelength removes Doppler and recoil shifts without giving up atom number, and this is what carries statistical and systematic uncertainty to about 1e-18. The claim has been checked independently: clocks at JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE and elsewhere agree when compared, which is the kind of reproducible experimental evidence I trust most. It is already enabling relativistic geodesy at the millimetre-to-centimetre scale, tests of constant variation and of the gravitational redshift, and dark-matter searches, and it underpins the planned redefinition of the second. The attribution is the cleanest of any shortlisted entry: Katori for the magic-wavelength concept and the first strontium demonstrations, Ye for taking the clock to record accuracy and stability and for the many-body clock physics. Seven of eight members ranked it, five in the top three, so it is also the entry on which our independent views overlap most. The prize would be for a decisive measurement tool plus its demonstrated scientific yield, rather than for a promise.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation, raised by Danielsson, Eriksson, Lindroth and Olsson in different ways, is overlap with earlier precision-metrology prizes: the 2005 prize for the frequency comb and laser-based precision spectroscopy and the 2012 prize for ion-trap control and clocks. Ye's comb-stabilised laser work sits close to the 2005 territory, and the lattice clock may look to some like an evolutionary step in the same programme. There is also a timing argument from Olsson that the applied payoff, the SI second redefinition, has not yet happened, and the scientific payoff in fundamental physics so far consists of tighter bounds rather than a discovery. Finally, other Sr-lattice contributors (Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Oates) are outside the two-name credit.

responses.point: Olsson ranks spherical-aberration correction (B053) first as an enabling instrument breakthrough that broke Scherzer's 1936 limit, with Rose, Urban and Haider as natural credit, while flagging that Krivanek's corrected-STEM work is omitted and that her own field's closeness raises a conflict risk.
responses.response: I agree with her criterion, since I weigh instruments that open a new way of observing nature in the same way, and B053 meets it. My difference is on the attribution and the evidence base. Both of us acknowledge the Krivanek priority question, and I cannot resolve it from this packet, so B053 carries a credit dispute that B027 does not. I would also like to know whether the committee regards aberration-corrected TEM as physics or as materials instrumentation. The lattice clock sits squarely in physics, and its performance claim, 1e-18 agreement between independent clocks, is verified by direct comparison rather than by image quality. I would keep B053 as a strong runner-up for the prize if the priority question is settled, but not as first choice. Note that it received only two ranks, from Olsson and Pearce.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED (B036) first as the architecture that unified microwave quantum optics with qubit control, and argues it complements rather than duplicates the 2025 prize for macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits.
responses.response: I put B036 seventh, and the disagreement is not about its importance. Circuit QED is the platform for superconducting processors and its toolbox is used everywhere. My concern is the recency of the 2025 prize on the same circuit platform, and my sense that the impact is more in engineering of an architecture than in a new observation of nature, though I accept that is arguable. Göran's reply that the physics, strong single-photon coupling and dispersive QND readout, is distinct from tunnelling is fair, and I do not dismiss it. I also note that he declares proximity, which is honest, and I will do the same on WACQT below. For me the case for a second circuits-related prize in two years is weaker than the case for a clock prize that has had twenty years to be tested across laboratories.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks topological insulators (B057) first as a clean, verified new class of matter, and sees the Kane-Mele plus Molenkamp trio as a defensible theory-plus-experiment configuration, while acknowledging the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang omission.
responses.response: I accept that the science is mature and the experimental confirmations (HgTe transport, ARPES in 3D materials) are convincing; seven of eight members ranked it but only two put it in the top three, which tells me enthusiasm is broad but not deep. My reservations are the 2016 topological-phases prize and the attribution problem: Bernevig and Zhang for the HgTe prediction, and Fu, Moore, Balents and Hasan for 3D, are outside the credited names, and Olle himself notes the boundary is arguable. I cannot judge band-theory priority as he can, so if he and Mehlig believe the three-name trio is robust I would defer on that point. I would still rank B027 ahead because its credit boundary is tighter.

responses.point: Pearce ranks the Higgs experimental discovery (B040) second, as a landmark detector and analysis achievement not recognised by the 2013 prize, but concedes any three-person selection from ATLAS and CMS is contestable.
responses.response: I ranked B040 sixth for the reason he gives himself: the science is beyond doubt, but the Statutes force a selection of three from thousands, and the choice among Della Negra, Jenni, Virdee and Gianotti is a judgement call. Pearce and I proposed different triples, which illustrates the problem. I do not think the committee should hold the discovery back for that reason alone, but until we have an agreed principle for crediting detector leadership, I would not build the prize around it. If the committee does want an experimental particle-physics part, I would want to see the other two members' view of Gianotti versus Della Negra.

uncertainties: Whether the committee reads the lattice clock as a new invention or as a continuation of the 2005 and 2012 metrology prizes.
Whether a lattice-clock prize is better timed after the SI second redefinition, as Olsson hints.
Whether Krivanek's contribution leaves B053 unresolved, which affects whether it is a serious alternative to B027.
How much weight the 2025 circuits prize should carry against B036 and, by extension, against B060 in a year following another quantum-technology prize.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict with B027 is apparent from my profile: no Lund colleague or collaborator is among Katori or Ye, and my advisor Svanberg and postdoc host Aldén are not involved. Two connections are worth noting. First, I am on the executive team of the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology, which is institutionally linked to Chalmers and to Göran Johansson, whose first choice is circuit QED; my own ranking of B036 should be read with that in mind, and I rank it low anyway. Second, my work on rare-earth crystals and quantum memories overlaps loosely with quantum-information candidates (B060, B036), but I have no personal tie to the credited names. My spin-off company Deep Light Vision has no connection with any shortlisted candidate.
